items.title: Bees die when they sting — and this makes evolutionary sense
items.claim: A worker bee that stings a mammal disembowels itself and dies. Sterile, suicidal workers shouldn't exist if natural selection works at the individual level. They do exist, abundantly.
items.prompt: How does evolution favour individuals that don't reproduce?

options.text: Natural selection doesn't really work for social insects

Hamilton's rule: a gene for altruism spreads if rB is greater than C (relatedness times benefit exceeds cost); worker bees share 75 percent of their genes with sisters due to haplodiploidy, so helping the queen reproduce passes on their own genes effectively
Queen bees control workers chemically against their interests

items.reveal:
W. D. Hamilton wrote the equation rB greater than C: a gene for helping behaviour spreads if the relatedness (r) times the benefit to the recipient (B) exceeds the cost to the actor (C).

In haplodiploid Hymenoptera (bees, ants, wasps), females are diploid (from a diploid mother and a haploid father), males are haploid (unfertilised eggs). A worker shares 50 percent of her genes with her own offspring (if she had any), but 75 percent with her full sisters — because their shared father is haploid and gave them ALL his genes.

So a worker's gene-propagation interest is best served by helping her mother (the queen) make more sisters. Sterility is rational from the gene's perspective.

Hamilton's work, building on J. B. S. Haldane's quip 'I would lay down my life for two brothers or eight cousins', founded sociobiology.
items.why: Selection is taught as acting on individuals. The gene's-eye view explains altruism, sociality and self-sacrifice — phenomena that the individual-level view can't easily handle.

items.title: Plants tell the date by measuring the LENGTH of the night
items.claim: Chrysanthemums flower in autumn. Spinach bolts in long-day summer. Plants 'know' the time of year. They don't measure day length — they measure how long the night is, by counting protein degradation events.
items.prompt: What molecules let plants measure night length?

options.text: Phytochromes — light-absorbing pigments that switch between two forms (Pr and Pfr); the ratio shifts in the dark by slow Pfr decay, and the time taken to reach a threshold tells the plant how long the night was

items.reveal:
Phytochrome exists in two interconverting forms: Pr (red-absorbing) and Pfr (far-red-absorbing). Red light (660 nm) converts Pr to Pfr; far-red light (730 nm) reverses it. In darkness, Pfr slowly degrades back to Pr.

Day-length detection works on NIGHT length. Interrupting a long night with a brief flash of red light is enough to convert Pr to Pfr and 'reset' the plant — and shows that the plant is timing darkness, not light. Far-red light reverses the effect (Borthwick, Hendricks 1950s).

Short-day plants (chrysanthemums, soybeans, rice) flower when nights exceed a critical length. Long-day plants (spinach, wheat, lettuce) flower when nights are shorter than a critical length. Day-neutral plants (tomatoes, sunflowers) flower at a certain age.

The signal travels from leaves to apical meristem. The mobile signal — long sought as 'florigen' (Chailakhyan 1937) — was finally identified in 2007 as the FT protein (FLOWERING LOCUS T).

Agricultural exploitation: greenhouses can artificially adjust day length to force flowering year-round. Cut-flower industries rely on photoperiod manipulation.
items.why: Plants seem time-blind. They use a beautiful molecular clock built from light-reversible pigments — and they care about the dark, not the light.
